subject: chemistry
title: Empirical and molecular formulae
key_idea: The empirical formula is the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms in a compound. The molecular formula shows the actual number of atoms in one molecule. Divide each mass by Ar to get moles, find the simplest ratio, then write the formula.

blocks.text: Two kinds of formula describe the same compound. This section covers what each shows.

items.meaning: The simplest whole-number ratio of the atoms of each element in a compound.
The actual number of atoms of each element in one molecule.

items: To get the empirical formula from a molecular formula, divide all the numbers by the largest number that goes into all of them.
Some compounds have the same empirical and molecular formula, such as water, H₂O.
From a diagram or model of a molecule, count the atoms of each element, then write the simplest ratio.
From a model of an ionic lattice, count the ions of each type. A lattice with 1 Mg²⁺ ion for every 2 Cl⁻ ions has the empirical formula MgCl₂.
Empirical formula = simplest whole-number ratio of atoms.
Molecular formula = the real number of atoms in a molecule.
A molecular formula is a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula.

blocks.text: You are given the mass of each element in a sample. Turn the masses into moles to find the ratio of atoms. Always show your working.

blocks.label: Moles of an element
where: Ar = relative atomic mass of the element

items.lead: Divide each mass by its Ar.

items.text: Divide both by the smaller number, 0.01. Sn : Cl = 1 : 4.

items: If the ratio is not whole numbers, such as 1 : 1.5, multiply both by 2 to get 2 : 3.
Do not divide Ar by mass. That inverts the ratio and gives the wrong formula.
If you are given percentages, treat them as masses in 100 g. For 85.7% C and 14.3% H: C is 85.7 ÷ 12 = 7.14 and H is 14.3 ÷ 1 = 14.3. The ratio is 1 : 2, so the formula is CH₂.
Mass ÷ Ar gives moles. Compare the moles.
Divide by the smallest number to get the ratio.
Turn the ratio into a formula with whole numbers.

blocks.text: If you know the empirical formula and the Mr of the compound, you can find the molecular formula.

items.lead: Find the Mr of the empirical formula.
items.text: A hydrocarbon has empirical formula CH₂ and Mr = 84. Mr of CH₂ = 12 + (2 × 1) = 14.
84 ÷ 14 = 6, so there are six CH₂ units.

diagram.alt: Practise finding the number of carbon atoms in a hydrocarbon from its empirical formula and Mr.
working: There are {answer} carbon atoms and twice as many hydrogen atoms in each molecule.
diagram.question: A hydrocarbon has the empirical formula CH₂ and a relative formula mass of **{M}**. How many carbon atoms are in one molecule? (Ar: C = 12, H = 1)

items: Divide the Mr of the compound by the Mr of the empirical formula.
Multiply every number in the empirical formula by the answer.
Show both steps in your working.

sections.heading: An experiment: the formula of magnesium oxide

blocks.text: You can find the empirical formula of magnesium oxide by measuring the masses of magnesium and oxygen that combine.

items.text: Find the mass of a crucible and lid. Add magnesium ribbon and weigh again.
Heat the crucible strongly. Lift the lid briefly so oxygen can get in.
Cool and weigh. Reheat and reweigh until the mass stops changing, which shows the magnesium has reacted completely.
The mass gained is the mass of oxygen. Find the moles of Mg and O and the simplest ratio.

items: Example: 0.24 g of Mg gains 0.16 g of oxygen. Mg: 0.24 ÷ 24 = 0.01. O: 0.16 ÷ 16 = 0.01.
The ratio is 1 : 1, so the empirical formula is MgO.
The gain in mass is the mass of oxygen.
Reheat until the mass is constant.
Then use moles to find the ratio.

checks.q: Give the empirical formula of a compound with the molecular formula C₆H₁₂O₆.
1.20 g of magnesium reacts completely with 3.55 g of chlorine. Calculate the empirical formula. (Ar: Mg = 24.0, Cl = 35.5)
checks.a: Mg: 1.20 ÷ 24.0 = 0.05. Cl: 3.55 ÷ 35.5 = 0.1. The ratio is 1 : 2. The formula is MgCl₂.

checks.q: In the magnesium oxide experiment, how do you check that all the magnesium has reacted?
checks.a: Reheat and weigh again, and repeat until the mass stays constant.

worked_example.question:
Tin reacts with chlorine to form tin chloride.

A sample of tin chloride contains 1.19 g of tin and 1.42 g of chlorine.

Calculate the empirical formula of this tin chloride.

(relative atomic masses: Cl = 35.5, Sn = 119.0)

You must show your working.
worked_example.tip: One mark each for the moles, the ratio and the formula.

worked_example.question:

The relative formula mass of the compound is 180.0.

What is the molecular formula of the compound?

Relative atomic mass (Ar): C = 12.0, H = 1.0, O = 16.0
